paper_title: Data World: Scaling Data Environments from Scratch

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Data agents use code to process heterogeneous files and derive analytical insights. Scaling their training faces costly environment curation, privacy and intellectual-property restrictions, and difficulty verifying open-ended findings without known generative truth. Our core insight is to specify the world behind the files before generating the files themselves. We introduce Data World, a multi-agent engine that synthesizes environments, tasks, and rubrics from explicit mechanisms. Independent audits check target recoverability from observed files; rubrics support evaluation and RL rewards. Human preference-based curation for question realism selects 100 tasks across 50 held-out worlds and 16 domains for DataWorld-Bench. The engine also yields 2,135 training tasks from 1,037 disjoint worlds. Evaluation of ten frontier models shows that the benchmark remains challenging, particularly for insight discovery, with a consistent computation-insight gap. RL-zero training on the synthesized tasks produces DataWorld-35B-A3B from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B without trajectory distillation. Under matched evaluation, it improves over its base by 7.06 points on DataWorld-Bench, 14.28 on DAComp, 20.90 on DABstep-Hard, and 12.13 on JobBench, a broader occupational benchmark.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Data agents use code to inspect heterogeneous files, compute quantities, and derive evidence-supported analytical insights (Huang et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2025). Their data environments often contain multisource structured data distributed across CSV and Figure 1: Supervision for data agents: exploration-based synthesis (top) versus Data World (bottom). Exploring existing files may leave valid findings without matching criteria; Data World specifies mechanisms first, aligning files and rubrics with analytical targets. Excel tables (Dong et al., 2026b; Hasegawa et al., 2026). task may ask an agent to explain change in an outcome or trace its downstream implications, requiring more than correct computation alone. Training and evaluating these agents therefore require both diverse environments for multistep analysis and feedback that distinguishes supported conclusions from errors. As agentic LLM post-training scales, this joint supply of environments and supervision becomes central constraint (Huang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026; Tu et al., 2026; Tian et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). Synthetic data has long served as an important complement to real data when the latter is costly or restricted (Walonoski et al., 2018). Yet for data agents, two obstacles limit this supply. First, diversity and accessibility: acquiring and annotating real workflows is costly, while privacy and intellectualproperty restrictions constrain reuse (Dong et al., 2026b; Walonoski et al., 2018). Second, verifiability: the data-generating process behind real files is often unavailable, so open-ended findings rely on curated references or approximate matching (Gu et al., 2024; Sahu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). Exploring these files to write tasks and rubrics ties supervision to what the curator or mining model discovers (Ramrakhya et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). For example, consider an expert or strong model given food-delivery records collected from an online platform and asked to write rubric for evaluating analyses of declining sales. Inspecting these records, it may identify expired promotions as contributor but overlook reduced restaurant opening hours. An agent uncovering the latter may then receive no credit because the rubric omits that explanation, even when the records support it. Indeed, ten experts or strong models could offer ten different explanations for the same decline, as data complexity and inadequately controlled confounders can leave the underlying mechanism ambiguous. How can we scale diverse data environments with grounded supervision while retaining open-ended analytical depth? Our core insight is to specify the world behind the files before generating the files themselves. Analysis depends on statistical and relational structure that explicit mechanisms can instantiate in code. This enables varied environments without private source records, while known generative states ground checks of selected analytical targets. Synthesizing new environments and task-specific answers also reduces the risk of pretraining contamination associated with reusing public datasets. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting difference for data agent: its targeted findings have aligned rubric criteria rather than depending on prior exploration of existing files. The key challenge is preserving target recoverability through imperfect observations without making the analysis trivial. We propose Data World, multi-agent synthesis engine that expands directed acyclic dependency graph (DAG) into world contract, generates canonical state layer by layer, and projects it into analyst-visible files. Independent agent sessions exchange read-only artifacts to preserve cross-layer consistency; separate auditor checks the specified relationships and target-phenomenon recoverability from imperfect observations. The generative record then grounds tasks and rubrics, while the solving agent receives only the task and observed files; rubrics distinguish data computation from insight discovery, and scoring against them supplies evaluation feedback and training rewards. Running this engine yields DataWorld-Bench, with 100 tasks from 50 held-out worlds across 16 domains, and world-disjoint RL training set of 2,135 tasks from 1,037 worlds. Evaluation of ten frontier models reveals consistent computationinsight gap, and RL-zero training with rubric rewards produces DataWorld-35B-A3B, which improves over its base on held-out worlds and three external benchmarks spanning data analysis and broader professional work. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce mechanism-first framework for synthesizing data environments, grounding task rubrics in canonical generative state and auditing the recoverability of target phenomena from imperfect observations. We derive DataWorld-Bench and worlddisjoint training set from this engine, using fine-grained rubrics to reveal computation insight gap across ten frontier models. We demonstrate training utility via RL-zero training on the synthesized tasks, without distilling trajectories from stronger models, yielding substantial gains over the base on held-out worlds and three external benchmarks.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Data analysis agents and benchmarks. Existing environments draw on Kaggle competitions, scientific datasets, government open data, and released enterprise records (Jing et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2024; Hasegawa et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026b). LLM data-agent benchmarks span text-toSQL over curated databases (Yu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023), code-driven analysis over files (Hu et al., 2024; Jing et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2024; Egg et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2025), and multi-table government or enterprise spreadsheet workflows (Hasegawa et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026b). Closest to our setting, open-ended insight-discovery benchmarks DiscoveryBench and BLADE for scientific discovery (Majumder et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2024), InsightBench and InsightEval for business analytics (Sahu et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2026)score the insights agents extract, but their environments come from available sources and their reference insights from expert annotation or model-based exploration. Data World complements these sourcebased benchmarks with mechanism-grounded criteria and audits of target-phenomenon recoverability. Task synthesis and rubric-based rewards. complementary line of work keeps the data real but synthesizes tasks by exploring it: agents probe an environment to propose diverse, feasible, and verifiable tasks (Ramrakhya et al., 2026), or mine insights from available datasets to build evaluation suites (Sahu et al., 2025). When the underlying generative process is unavailable, scaling challenging open-ended tasks alongside dependable supervision requires additional curation or evaluation machinery (Gu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026). Rubric-derived rewards scored by LLM judges extend reinforcement learning to open-ended tasks (Gunjal et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025b; Wei et al., 2026). Our rubrics are instead written against generative record with independent audit results: the judge still interprets responses, but specified criteria can be cross-checked against that record and the observed files. This limits dependence on an annotators or mining models ability to discover the targeted insight from existing data, without removing biases in mechanism design, rubric selection, or judging. Synthetic environments and data. Environments are widely seen as the bottleneck of agent post-training (Huang et al., 2025a), yet early interactive environments such as WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024) and τ -bench (Yao et al., 2025) are handcurated and hard to scale. Recent pipelines synthesize environments for MCP-based tool-use agents in different ways. Agent World Model (Wang et al., 2026) and ScaleEnv (Tu et al., 2026) grow simulated tools, databases, and tasks from platform names or domain keywords, without assuming API documentation or predefined tasks. EnvScaler (Song et al., 2026) and ASTRA (Tian et al., 2026) distill environments from existing trajectories and task sets, while EnvFactory (Xu et al., 2026) and Agent-World (Dong et al., 2026a) assemble environments from web-found MCP interfaces. In contrast, Data World targets terminal-based analysis of interdependent files, with specified generative relationships for auditing analytical findings rather than simulated tool APIs. Synthetic data methods such as GReaT, SDV, and REaLTabFormer learn from existing databases (Borisov et al., 2023; Patki et al., 2016; Solatorio and Dupriez, 2023); Synthea simulates records from explicit mechanisms (Walonoski et al., 2018), and synthetic causal benchmarks target causal discovery (Ferdous et al., 2025). Our focus is the recoverability of analytical targets across imperfect, interdependent files.

sections.title: 3.4 Benchmark and Training-Set Curation
sections.content: Of 1,302 candidate worlds, we retain 1,087: 1,037 training worlds yielding 2,135 RL tasks and 50 held-out worlds yielding 100 test tasks across all 16 domains. Test worlds are entirely excluded from training and must pass every audit check; training worlds have 95.98% DAG-edge pass rate. For GPT-6-Astra leads overall and in computation, Qwen-3.8-Max-0902 leads in insight discovery and ranks second overall, and GPT-6.1-Sol ranks second in computation and third overall. Every model shows computationinsight gap (4.87 21.35 points), indicating that strong data processing does not automatically yield targeted analytical conclusions. These comparisons concern rubricdefined skills, however, and criterion coverage and scoring differences may contribute to the gap. Interaction cost does not uniformly track performance: GPT-6-Astra leads overall with the fewest rounds, while Kimi-K3 uses the fewest total and response tokens. Qwen-3.8-Max-0902 achieves the highest insight score with the largest token usage; GPT-6.1-Sol attains similar overall score with fewer rounds and tokens. MiniMax-M3 takes the most rounds yet scores lowest, so longer interaction alone is not sufficient for stronger analysis. These cross-model comparisons do not isolate the benefit of additional inference, as models also differ in capability and interaction strategy. Negative rubric items capture demonstrably wrong calculations or contradicted conclusions  (Table 2)  . GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra have the highest shares of trajectories without such items, while Gemini-3.8-Flash and MiniMax-M3 trigger them most often. Both GPT models trigger negative items less often than Qwen-3.8-Max-0902 but score lower in insight discovery, distinguishing avoidance of incorrect conclusions from recovery of targeted findings. After removing each models mean, domain analyses identify bioinformatics, operations, and energy as relatively easier and transportation, environment, and education as harder (Section A.3.3), motivating evaluation across diverse domains rather than aggregate scores alone; small per-domain task counts preclude within-domain model rankings. No model shows detectable causeconsequence difficulty difference at the achieved resolution (Section A.3.4), providing no evidence that either graph route is systematically easier.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: The mechanism-first design is useful for data agents only if the generated files support meaningful analysis and the associated rubrics provide useful learning signals. We therefore evaluate two questions: what computational and insightdiscovery capabilities DataWorld-Bench reveals in existing agents, and whether training on separate synthesized worlds improves performance on heldout worlds and external benchmarks.

This long-context, multi-turn interaction pattern resembles that documented in MiMos public RL training logs (Xiaomi MiMo Team, 2026). These results indicate that RL training on fully synthesized environments preserves the base models general language and coding capabilities, and that purely synthetic supervision does not noticeably disturb its factual world knowledge.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: Data World offers data-centric route to scalable, verifiable supervision for data agents by specifying generative mechanisms before synthesizing observations and auditing analytical targets. Separating canonical truth from analyst-visible files grounds supervision in known mechanisms while requiring agents to recover findings from observations alone. The engine yields DataWorld-Bench for measuring the computationinsight gap and world-disjoint set for RL-zero training; gains extend to unseen worlds, external data-analysis tasks, and broader occupational workflows, without task-solving demonstrations from stronger models. This joint synthesis expands task supply without requiring curators to rediscover each targeted finding from the generated files. Together, these results support mechanismgrounded environment synthesis as scalable complement to real-world data, providing both evaluation criteria and training signals.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: First, the tight coupling among synthesis components and the cost of regenerating worlds and tasks limit exhaustive ablations. We do not construct multiple controlled variants of the world and task synthesis pipeline, so our results support the utility of the framework as whole rather than isolate the contribution of each component. Moreover, the central claim concerns what synthesis from scratch enablesverifiable, scalable supervisionrather than the optimality of any particular component, so adding, removing, or fine-tuning individual components is unlikely to yield materially better outcome: weakening the pipelines coherence would sacrifice the auditability and coverage that motivate the design. Synthesized environments and tasks are intended to complement, not replace, real-world data; we do not compare which source is more effective. Second, fully synthetic tasks may differ from the questions human users pose to AI agents in practice. Although human preference-based curation selects benchmark questions for realism, it does not establish that the resulting tasks represent the distribution of real user requests, particularly their ambiguity, implicit context, and evolving goals. Third, mechanism-grounded rubrics do not exhaust all valid analytical findings, and LLM-based grading may introduce judge bias. Audited generative truth makes the specified criteria verifiable, but does not guarantee that alternative insights receive appropriate credit or that scores remain consistent across different judging models.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Environment synthesis and scaling for agent training have recently become active research areas, with many concurrent contributions appearing in rapid succession. Due to page constraints and the limits of our knowledge, we cite and discuss only the most closely related work known to us; we regret any relevant omissions. AI agents construct environments and rubrics, and an LLM judge scores responses under the access restrictions described in Section 3. These artifacts and scores do not establish suitability for real-world decisions: audits verify specified relationships and recoverability, while human curation assesses question realism rather than operational validity. Although synthesis reduces reliance on private records, outputs should still be reviewed for sensitive or proprietary content before release. Use in consequential domains requires independent validation and human oversight. AI tools were also used to assist with code development and manuscript writing; the authors reviewed, edited, and validated all generated content and take full responsibility for the correctness of the code and the manuscript.

A.2 Evaluated Models We evaluate ten models on DataWorld-Bench  (Table 1)  . The descriptions below summarize their public technical reports, model cards, and system cards. All ten use the mini-swe-agent harness (SWE-bench Team, 2025), lightweight harness that exposes bash as its sole tool and follows ReAct-style loop, interleaving model reasoning, shell-command execution, and feedback from command outputs. GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026b) is OpenAIs flagship reasoning model in the GPT-6 family for complex, tool-using workflows. Its system card describes reinforcement-learning-based reasoning training and improved robustness to prompt injection and unauthorized actions in agentic settings. GPT-6.1-Sol (OpenAI, 2026a) is OpenAIs efficiency-oriented model in the GPT-6.1 family. OpenAI reports capabilities comparable to GPT-6 Astra with improved speed and affordability; its system-card addendum states that it uses the same types of data and training as Astra. Qwen-3.8-Max-0902 (Alibaba Qwen Team, 2026b) is Alibabas largest Qwen model: 2.4Tparameter mixture-of-experts with 95B activated per token, 1M-token context window, and multimodal input (text, image, and video). The 0902 snapshot (released 2026-09-02) upgrades the August Qwen3.8-Max release specifically for coding and agent performance; Alibaba reports fifth place in Text Arena and second in Vision Arena for the base release, and its open weights have become popular base for coding agents. Kimi-K3 (Moonshot AI, 2026) is Moonshot AIs open-weight flagship and the first open 3Tclass model: 2.8T-parameter mixture-of-experts with 896 experts (top-16 routing), KDA attention, 1M-token context window, and native multimodality. Its technical report documents frontier-level performance across long-horizon coding, agentic, knowledge, and reasoning evaluations; third-party tracking places it at #3 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (Artificial Analysis, 2026), and it attains an Elo of 1668 on GDPval-AA v2 (Patwardhan et al., 2026) for agentic office work. HY4-Preview (Tencent Hunyuan Team, 2026) is Tencent Hunyuans most capable open model to date: 770B-parameter MoE with 49B activated parameters (256 routed experts plus one shared expert, top-8 routing) and 1M-token context window, released under Apache 2.0. Tencent reports its largest generation-over-generation gain so far, with the biggest improvements on long-horizon software engineering, document-heavy office work, and scientific research. In blind evaluations of 203 real engineering tasks rated by 163 experts, HY4Preview averaged 2.99/4.00, edging out GLM 5.3 (2.92; 46.8% wins vs. 40.4% losses) and Kimi-K3 (2.94; 51.2% wins vs. 40.9% losses). GLM 5.3 (Zhipu AI, 2026) is Zhipu AIs (Z.ai) coding-focused flagship: 743B model sharing the GLM-5.2 backbone with substantially upgraded post-training run. Z.ai reports it as the most capable open-weights model for coding, with 50% improvement over GLM-5.2 on its in-house Z.ai Code Bench, and highlights emergent defensivecybersecurity capabilities alongside strong performance on long-horizon autonomous engineering tasks. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) targets extreme long-context serving efficiency: 552B backbone built on Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED) architecture with 8B prefill and 16B decode activated parameters and 1M-token context. Its technical report pushes KV cache compression across architecture, numeric precision, and deployment jointly, reducing the global (always-in-HBM) KV cache footprint to 890 bytes per tokenabout 4 smaller than DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 437 smaller than DeepSeek-V1. Gemini-3.8-Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026) is Google DeepMinds lightweight, API-only entry in the Gemini 3.8 family. Despite its size class, it is reported to lead Harveys Legal Agent Benchmark and to score 90.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) (vs. 81.6% for its 3.7 Flash predecessor); companion Flash Cyber variant improves recall by 7.59.7% on an internal penetration-testing benchmark at 2.35.2 lower cost. This environment follows the Hillcats 2026 game-day supply operations, linking plant utilization and quality inspections with procurement, warehouse inventories, shipments, and ballpark availability. A.5 RL Evaluation Protocol This section details the evaluation settings behind Table 3, with paired comparisons focused on DataWorld-35B-A3B versus its base. We evaluate the models on four benchmarks that probe complementary data-agent abilities: JobBench, which tests source-grounded professional reasoning across broad range of occupations (Li et al., 2026); DAComp, which measures open-ended data-science task solving graded by LLM judges; DABstep-Hard, which tests multi-step reasoning over real-world tabular data with strictly verifiable answers; and the held-out split of our own DataWorld-Bench, which stresses open-ended data computation and insight discovery inside fully executable worlds. A.5.1 Shared Evaluation and Scoring automatic correctness checks, while DataWorldBench applies its own rubrics with the same Gemini-3.8-Flash judge. For the judge-graded DAComp and DataWorld-Bench tasks, scores come from single judging pass and are scaled by 100 for display; DataWorld-Bench normalizes net rubric points to [0, 1], while DAComp retains its native scoring. DABstep-Hard instead uses binary correctness. Tables 3 and 1 use the same DataWorld-Bench judge, rubrics, and single-pass scoring procedure for archived reports, so their DataWorld-Bench scores share the same scoring scale. The tables cover distinct sets of evaluated models; Gemini-3.8-Flash is the shared judge, not an overlapping evaluated model. The comparisons in Table 3 are internally consistent because each pair shares the same benchmark-specific scoring procedure. A.5.2 Paired Statistical Analysis Tasks are paired one-to-one by identical task name across the two systems, and is the per-task difference DataWorld-35B-A3B base. The paired analysis covers DAComp, DABstep-Hard, and DataWorld-Bench, with 200, 378, and 100 complete pairs, respectively; no task is dropped from these pairings. The paired one-sample test on the per-task differences yields the minimum detectable difference MDE = 2.802 s/ n, the same formula used in Section A.3.4. A.5.3 Benchmark-Specific Details JobBench (n = 65) (Li et al., 2026) evaluates agents on professional work tasks that domain experts most want delegated, spanning 35 occupations from office support to management and life science.
